opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think there's one clean answer. There are genuine benefits on both sides.

The case for concentration is that safety research is collaborative. You learn a lot by being in the room with other people working on the same problems: sharing half-formed ideas, getting quick feedback, building on each other's tooling. A lot of the most useful work needs access to frontier models and serious compute, and it really helps when the safety team sits close to the people training those models. You can influence decisions early instead of reviewing something after it's basically done. If you scatter people too thinly, you can end up with one or two safety-minded people at each lab who don't have the leverage or support to change much, and who may burn out fighting the same battles alone.

On the other hand, there's a strong argument for having safety-minded people everywhere frontier development happens. The risks don't care which company builds the system. If one lab has a great safety culture and another doesn't, the world is only as safe as the least careful actor. Having people inside different organisations means you get different perspectives, a bit of a check on groupthink, and someone in each place who can push for good practices, raise concerns, and help with things like sharing evaluations or norms across the industry.

How I personally weigh it: I'd ask what the marginal person actually does in each place. Do they have real influence on training and deployment decisions? Do they have colleagues they can learn from and who support them? Is leadership receptive? Someone very senior with a strong track record might do enormous good as a voice inside a company that has fewer safety people. Someone earlier in their career might benefit a lot from being on a strong team where they can grow quickly and contribute to research that gets published and used more widely.

It's also worth remembering that a lot of good safety research isn't company-specific. Interpretability techniques, evaluation methods, and alignment approaches can be published and adopted by others. So even a concentrated team can have broad impact if the work gets shared and becomes an industry standard.

So I'd encourage people not to think of it as purely "join the best team" versus "spread out," but to ask honestly where they'd have the most leverage, given their skills and the specific environment they'd be walking into.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think there are real arguments on both sides.

The case for concentration is pretty straightforward. Safety research benefits enormously from working at the frontier, so you want to be at a place that has the most capable models. And a lot of the research is quite collaborative: you want to be able to walk over to someone who did the pretraining run and ask why the model is behaving a certain way, or pair with an interpretability person on a weird phenomenon you've noticed. There are also compounding effects — a critical mass of safety researchers shapes the culture of the organization, which influences deployment decisions, what gets prioritized, how seriously the leadership takes a concerning eval result. If you have one safety researcher at a company, they're mostly just producing papers. If you have fifty, they can actually change what the company does.

That's roughly the Anthropic thesis, honestly. The bet is that having a frontier lab where safety is the organizing principle, rather than a team bolted onto the side, produces something different than what you'd get from distributing the same people across the industry.

But I want to be fair to the other side, because I think the case for spreading out is also real. If the most dangerous outcome comes from whichever lab is least careful, then it matters a lot that every frontier lab has some people internally who understand the risks and have standing to push back. An outsider publishing a paper doesn't have the same influence as someone in the room when a deployment decision is being made. And there's a diversity-of-approaches argument too — if everyone's at one place, you get one research culture, one set of blind spots.

How I'd actually weigh it: I think the default pull for a lot of people is to want to be where the action is, and that's not a bad instinct, but I'd push back a little on the idea that it's always the right call. A few things I'd consider. One, how much of your impact comes from the research itself versus from your influence on the organization? If it's the research, concentration probably wins because you'll do better work with better collaborators and better infrastructure. If it's the influence, then being somewhere that has fewer people like you might matter more. Two, what's the marginal value of one more safety person at each place? That's genuinely hard to estimate from outside, but it's probably decreasing at the places that already have a lot. And three, honestly, where will you personally be effective and not miserable? People burn out when they feel like they're constantly fighting the organization, and a burned-out safety researcher isn't helping anyone.

My overall take is that the field is probably still somewhat under-concentrated in the sense that there aren't enough places where safety has real institutional weight, and I'd rather see a couple of labs where it's deeply embedded than a thin layer everywhere. But I wouldn't want everyone to make the same call, and I think a reasonable person could land on the other side of this.

astra-6.text:
I think there are real benefits in both directions. If you’re one safety researcher in an organisation where nobody else is thinking about these problems, it can be hard to make progress. Having colleagues who share your concerns, who can challenge your ideas, and who can help turn research into changes in how models are built and deployed is really valuable.

But there’s also a strong argument for having people at each of the companies that might build very powerful AI. A lot of the relevant knowledge is specific to the organisation: what its models can do, how decisions get made, and where there are opportunities to improve safety. Someone working elsewhere won’t necessarily have that access or influence.

So I’d think about this in terms of building strong teams at multiple places. And the marginal choice depends on the situation. Are you joining a team where you’ll learn a lot and become much more effective? Or could you help establish a serious safety effort somewhere that otherwise wouldn’t have one? I don’t think there’s a single allocation that’s right independently of the people and the organisations involved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are real benefits in both directions. If you’re one safety researcher in an organisation where nobody else is thinking about these problems, it can be very difficult to make progress. Having a group of people who can challenge your assumptions, build on your work, and turn an idea into something the company actually uses is really valuable. So I wouldn’t aim to spread people evenly across companies regardless of whether they’ll have a productive team around them.

But there’s also a strong case for having good safety teams at several frontier companies. They have access to different models, they can influence different decisions, and they can pursue different approaches. If everyone is concentrated in one place, you’re putting a lot of weight on that organisation’s judgement and on its approach turning out to be right.

So my instinct is to favour a few strong groups across different organisations, with substantial communication between them. And for an individual researcher, I’d put a lot of weight on the specifics: who will you work with, what will you be able to study, and is there a credible path for your research to affect what gets deployed?
